title: I Created a (terrible) Video Game Console
beats: Shelf of beginner-kit electronics, decision to build a game console; Arduino introduced as a tiny computer with pins that output or read voltage
Joystick: knows potentiometer from volume knobs but not how it relates; does research on camera
Wiper turning along resistive track; battery across outer terminals gives voltage zero to max, so voltage tells knob angle
Wire one pot to pin 0, write a script that reads and prints voltage, upload; turn knob and watch number rise
Value goes to 1023, not a thousand volts; 5 V mapped to 10-bit integer
Swap in joystick, second wire, normalise to -1 to +1 because it makes more sense
Cheapest display: 8x8 LED matrix via a library; second display for widescreen joke
Buzzer: alternate high and low, or tone function; build a Unity editor with sine wave to write music; result annoying, scrapped
Prototype; snake; C++ is similar enough to C# so he reuses what he knows
Shows engine code; per-LED set was 15 ms per frame so buffer rows as bits and send in one go
Pointers and memory addresses confusing; second game follows
Blender models, 3-tier balsa case, wires, breadboard explained in one sentence; cover glued wrong way twice
Paint it yellow, told it looks like a monster, add eyebrows and teeth
It works; try 9 V battery, silence, then taped AA batteries work
Admits the result is wired-together pre-built parts in a poor box but is proud; thanks

theory: This is a project vlog rather than an explainer: understanding is delivered as a side effect of the build, with each component studied only just before it is used and verified on the spot. The humility and visible failure keep stakes low, which probably makes a beginner kit feel approachable. Depth is intentionally shallow; the transferable bit is learn-just-in-time then test on the real device.
